name: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
question: Should I change the prompt, the context or the weights?
summary: Most problems are solved without touching weights. Change the prompt when instructions or examples are missing; add retrieval when the model needs facts, especially facts that change; fine-tune when you need consistent behaviour, format, style or a narrow skill at high volume, and have good examples. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour better than knowledge: tuning on new facts can even raise hallucination.
useCases: When a vendor proposes training a model on your documents
When prompt and RAG results have plateaued on evals

items.detail: instructions, examples and structured outputs are cheapest to change
facts, documents and anything that changes; cite sources
format, tone, style, a narrow skill, or shorter prompts at scale
a tuned model that reads retrieved context well
fixed costs of tuning only pay off at high volume
retune when the base model or the task changes

steps: Measure the prompted baseline on a real eval set
Ask what is missing: instructions, knowledge or behaviour
Try the cheapest fix first and measure again
Fine-tune only with enough good examples, enough volume and an owner for upkeep
pitfalls: Fine-tuning to “teach” facts that change monthly
Skipping a strong prompt baseline, so gains are overstated
Forgetting the cost of retuning when the base model is retired
tools: Amazon Bedrock and Vertex AI tuning
remember: Prompt for instructions, retrieve for facts, tune for behaviour.
caption: Illustrative rules; measure your own baseline first.

code.text: bar = task.required_accuracy               # from a real eval set
return "rag" if task.needs_facts else "prompt + better examples"
return "rag + fine-tuned model"        # tune behaviour, retrieve facts
# Re-run this when the base model, prices or the task change

steps.title: Measure a baseline and set the bar
steps.text: The insurer built 500 real questions with checked answers before choosing anything. Without that, every option “seems to work”.

steps.title: Try the prompt first
steps.text: A structured prompt with examples and structured outputs is the cheapest change and the easiest to undo. It answered 71% here.

steps.title: Facts go in retrieval
steps.text: Policy wordings change, and answers need citations. Retrieval over the current PDFs reached 93%; tuning on them reached 76% and went stale.

steps.title: Tuning has to pay for itself
steps.text: Training, evaluation, hosting and retraining are fixed costs. Below about 100,000 calls a month, or without a thousand good examples, they are rarely recovered.

steps.title: Tune for behaviour, retrieve facts
steps.text: When the gap is format, tone or a narrow skill, tuning helps. When both matter, a tuned model reads retrieved context.

steps.title: Revisit the decision
steps.text: A new base model can make a tuned one obsolete, and a price change can move the break-even. Re-run the comparison.

practice.scenario: An Indian insurer was offered a project to fine-tune a model on its policy wordings so its agent would “know the products”. The team measured first. A structured prompt answered 71% of 500 real questions correctly, and adding retrieval over the current policy PDFs raised that to 93%, with citations. Fine-tuning on the wordings reached only 76% and went stale when two products were revised the next month. They kept retrieval and later tuned a small model for tone only.

industries.use: Policy questions: retrieval for wordings that change, tuning only for tone
Fee and limit questions change with every circular, so they belong in retrieval
Clinical note formatting at scale suits tuning; drug facts belong in retrieval

practice.analogy: A new employee: give them a clear brief (prompt), a well-indexed handbook they can look things up in (retrieval), and training only for the skills they will use every day (fine-tuning). You would not make them memorise a price list that changes each month.

numericDrill.question: Answering with RAG on a large model costs ₹0.55 a query. A fine-tuned small model costs ₹0.10 a query plus ₹60,000 a month for training refreshes, evaluation and hosting. Above what monthly volume is the tuned model cheaper?
numericDrill.answer: Set 0.55v = 0.10v + 60,000, so 0.45v = 60,000 and v ≈ 133,333 queries a month. Below that, the fixed cost of tuning is not recovered, before counting the engineering time to keep it current.

interview.question: When would you fine-tune rather than use RAG?
interview.answer: When the gap is behaviour rather than knowledge: a consistent format, tone or narrow skill, or a shorter prompt at high volume, and you have enough good examples. Facts, especially ones that change, belong in retrieval, where they can be updated and cited. The two combine well: a tuned model that reads retrieved context.

interview.question: Why not fine-tune a model on your documents so it knows them?
interview.answer: Fine-tuning is poor at adding new facts reliably, the facts go stale as documents change, and the model cannot cite a source. Research has found that tuning on unfamiliar facts can even raise hallucination. Retrieval updates instantly and shows where each answer came from.

mistakes.mistake: Tuning on facts that change every month
mistakes.fix: Put them in retrieval and cite sources

mistakes.mistake: Comparing a tuned model with a weak prompt
mistakes.fix: Beat the best prompted and RAG baseline first

quiz.question: An assistant gets policy details wrong, and the wordings are revised every quarter. What is the best first fix?
options: Retrieval over the current wordings, with citations
quiz.explanation: Facts that change belong in retrieval, where they can be updated and cited.

quiz.question: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to teach a model fees that change monthly?
options: The facts go stale and the model cannot cite a source
quiz.explanation: Weights are frozen at training time; retrieval reflects the current schedule.

quiz.question: Product descriptions must follow a strict brand voice across 2 million SKUs a year. Prompting reaches 78% on the style rubric. What is most likely to help?
options: Fine-tuning on a few thousand approved descriptions
quiz.explanation: Consistent style at high volume is the classic case for tuning.

quiz.question: What should you build before choosing between prompting, RAG and fine-tuning?
options: An eval set of real cases with checked answers
quiz.explanation: Without a baseline measurement every option “seems to work”.

quiz.question: RAG costs ₹0.55 a query; a tuned small model costs ₹0.10 plus ₹60,000 a month fixed. Roughly above what monthly volume is tuning cheaper?
Which gaps suit fine-tuning better than retrieval? Select all that apply.
options: A drug formulary that changes monthly
A concise clinical tone at high volume
quiz.explanation: Format and tone are behaviour; changing facts belong in retrieval or tools.

quiz.question: What did Gekhman et al. (2024) find about fine-tuning on new knowledge?
options: New facts are learned slowly and can raise hallucination
quiz.explanation: Unfamiliar facts are learned slowly and encourage hallucination.

quiz.question: A tuned model is proposed for 8,000 queries a month. What is the usual objection?
options: Fixed training and hosting costs are unlikely to be recovered
Tuned models cannot run at low volume
quiz.explanation: Volume must be high enough to pay back fixed costs.

quiz.question: When would you combine RAG with a fine-tuned model?
options: When you need current facts and a specific behaviour at scale
quiz.explanation: Retrieve the facts, tune the behaviour.

quiz.question: A strong prompt meets the accuracy bar. What should you do?
options: Keep the prompt: it is the cheapest option that works
quiz.explanation: The cheapest option that meets the bar wins.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a hidden cost of fine-tuning?
options: Retraining when the base model is retired
quiz.explanation: Prompt edits are cheap; the others recur with tuning.

quiz.question: A model gives wrong answers because the syllabus is not in its context. What is the gap?
quiz.explanation: Missing information is a knowledge gap: retrieval.

quiz.question: Which should you check before approving a tuning project? Select all that apply.
options: A strong prompted and RAG baseline on real cases
quiz.explanation: Baselines and data decide whether tuning can help.

quiz.question: Why might a tuned model need retraining later?
options: The base model is retired or the task changes
quiz.explanation: Upkeep is part of the cost of tuning.

quiz.question: A vendor promises that tuning on your help pages will make the bot “know the business”. The best response?
options: Measure RAG first; tuning adds facts poorly and they go stale
Tune on customer chats instead of anything else
quiz.explanation: Knowledge gaps are fixed by retrieval first.

quiz.question: Structured outputs already produce valid JSON. Is fine-tuning needed for format?
quiz.explanation: Constrained decoding solves many format problems without training.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of trying the prompt first?
options: It is cheapest and easiest to change or undo
It is always the most accurate
quiz.explanation: Low cost and reversibility.

quiz.question: Tuning scored 97% and RAG 77% on a style task. Which statement is right?
options: The gap was behaviour, so tuning fits
quiz.explanation: Style is behaviour.

quiz.question: An assistant’s answers are correct but too long. Which is the cheapest first try?
options: A prompt with a length limit and examples
quiz.explanation: Try the prompt before training.

quiz.question: Which kind of fact is safest to leave to a tuned model’s weights?
quiz.explanation: Only stable knowledge; anything that changes belongs in retrieval or tools.
